sections.title: Guidance overview

summary.text: Places the document within WHO's Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data, which promotes standardized core indicators, analyses and dashboards across programmes. It describes the toolkit's components and explains that this guidance offers district and facility managers examples of using routine data for decisions, without covering district management in full.

sections.extract: WHO TOOLKIT FOR ANALYSIS AND USE OF ROUTINE HEALTH FACILITY DATA This document is part of the WHO Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data – a set of capacity- building resources to optimize the analysis and use of data collected from health facilities through routine health information systems (RHIS). The Toolkit is a collaborative effort by multiple WHO technical programmes and partners. It

sections.title: Learning objectives

summary.text: States the learning objectives of the guidance: a focused set of indicators in three groups, standard visualizations in integrated dashboards and their use in meetings and supervision. It defines the target audience of district managers and analysts and lists suggested reading.

sections.extract: This guidance illustrates integrated analysis of RHIS data at district and facility levels. It aims to build understanding and skills in a recommended analytic approach that: y focuses on a minimum set of indicators organized into three cross-cutting groups; y uses standard visualizations to facilitate data interpretation: charts and tables organized into integrated dashboards that can be automatically updated in

sections.title: District health system

summary.text: Describes the district health system as a network of primary care facilities under a district hospital and management team, possibly including private providers, and explains how the term is used in the guidance.

sections.extract: Districts are administrative units. They come in all shapes and sizes, from a few thousand people to multi-million populations. In many countries, districts are the main subnational administrative unit and the level that manages the public health service delivery system. According to the WHO, the district health system [5] is “a network of primary care health facilities that deliver a comprehensive range of

sections.title: Data needs of district and facility managers

summary.text: Lists the responsibilities of district and facility managers, such as meeting policies, responding to events, ensuring access and using resources efficiently, and their need for routine data and context to fulfil them.

sections.extract: District and facility managers are responsible for ensuring that the health services under their management are appropriately delivered. This may include ensuring that: y district health services are in line with national and subnational policies, priorities and standards; y district health services quickly detect and respond to unusual events and changing needs; y all segments of the district population have

sections.title: Data sources at subnational level

summary.text: Explains that the guidance focuses on aggregate routine health information system data while noting other sources within the broader health information system, such as surveys, censuses and surveillance.

sections.extract: This guidance focuses on aggregate data reported through the RHIS. However, at district and facility levels, health information may be available from various sources as part of the broader country health information system (HIS). The HIS brings together data from multiple sources, including the RHIS, health facility assessments, client experience surveys, household surveys, censuses, civil registration systems,

sections.title: Routine health information system (RHIS)

summary.text: Describes the routine data that health facilities collect and report on diseases, service outputs and outcomes, and how often they are reported. It also outlines related information systems, including surveillance, human resources, logistics and financial management systems.

sections.extract: Health facilities routinely collect data on the diseases and other health conditions for which people seek care. They also collect routine data on facility activities (outputs such as number of outpatient department visits, number of vaccine doses given) and the outcomes of those activities (e.g. number of tuberculosis (TB) patients cured, number of inpatient deaths). These data are aggregated and reported at

sections.title: Population data

summary.text: Discusses the difficulty of obtaining reliable population denominators, especially for facility catchment areas, and recommends analyses that avoid them, such as trends in absolute numbers and facility-based denominators. It also notes other information sources that help interpret district data.

sections.extract: Population data serve as denominators for many RHIS indicators, e.g. utilization rates, coverage. It is important that all managers and analysts have an estimate of the population that the district system is expected to cover. However, there are often challenges in obtaining reliable population data. Population estimates based on projections of census data may be out-of-date or inaccurate; in general, the smaller

sections.title: Principles of this guidance

summary.text: Introduces the five principles behind the guidance, building on the toolkit's general principles and national-level documents.

sections.extract: This guidance is based on concepts and indicators presented in the Toolkit documents General principles and Integrated health services analysis: national level. These documents include detailed discussions on data analysis concepts and individual indicators. The focus of the district and facility level guidance is on practical data analysis needs at these operational levels of the health system. The data analysis

sections.title: Focused analysis - using a limited set of indicators

summary.text: Explains the principles of integration across programmes and of focusing on a limited set of tracer indicators to flag problems. It also discusses keeping disaggregation manageable to protect data quality, noting that WHO does not recommend sex disaggregation of routine childhood immunization data.

sections.extract: 3. Standardization – of indicators, analyses and visualizations 4. Data quality assessment – along with analysis 5. Purpose-oriented analysis – for management and planning 1.4.1 Integration – across programmes and services To make informed decisions, district managers need data that reflect performance across a wide range of domains and programmes: from coverage of immunization to utilization of financial resources.

sections.title: Standardization - of indicators, analyses and visualizations

summary.text: Describes standardizing indicators, analyses and visualizations so data can be compared, and introduces sample dashboards for facility and district levels over monthly and annual timeframes. It warns against cluttered electronic dashboards and stresses assessing and acknowledging data quality alongside analysis.

sections.extract: Standardization of data elements and indicators enables comparison over time and among places, populations and programmes. The way the indicators are visualized can also be standardized: a set of standard charts, tables, etc. can be defined and grouped in a standard dashboard. This document presents a sample set of standard dashboards for integrated health services analysis. There are dashboards for two analysis

sections.title: Purpose-oriented analysis - for management and planning

summary.text: Explains that routine data should inform short-term decisions from recent months and longer-term planning from yearly trends, with a framework table linking analysis types to management actions such as redeploying resources or adjusting supervision.

sections.extract: The purpose of RHIS data is to facilitate management decision-making. This guidance offers recommendations for analysis of RHIS data to support decisions taken at district and facility levels. Analysis of data from recent months should inform short-term decisions, while review of year-to-year trends helps to guide longer-term planning. sections.title: Analysis, interpretation and communication of RHIS findings
Ways to analyse RHIS data

summary.text: Explains how to clean routine data and analyse it through comparisons over time, between diseases, among facilities and against populations or targets. It describes suitable charts and tables for answering questions of when, who, what and where, with guidance on interpreting trends and outliers. A country example from Sierra Leone shows how simple tracking of immunization at facility level improved measles coverage.

sections.extract: Raw data are rarely suitable for decision-making. They cannot be interpreted easily and may even be misleading. First, the data should be “cleaned” – reviewed for completeness and consistency and, where possible, corrected. The data can then be visualized and analysed using charts and tables to enable easy identification and interpretation of key findings. Most analyses involve some form of comparison: comparison

sections.title: Interpretation and communication of RHIS data findings - regular review meetings and dashboar

summary.text: Describes how regular district review meetings and the distribution of printed dashboards can involve a wide range of staff in interpreting routine data. It covers meeting participants, preparation and follow-up, and ways of sending dashboards to facilities and managers as feedback.

sections.extract: review meetings and dashboard dissemination It may be possible for a small number of dedicated workers in the district health office and in each facility to complete all the tasks described in this guidance: data quality assurance; configuration of the charts and tables; review and interpretation of the dashboards; further investigations; and decision-making. Lupara district database

summary.text: Introduces the fictitious "Lupara" district Excel database used to demonstrate the sample dashboards, explaining that its data are adapted and do not represent any real place or good data quality. It describes the dashboard naming scheme by level, timeframe and indicator group. The section ends with review questions asking readers to compare different dashboards.

sections.extract: This guidance provides sample dashboards for a fictitious district called “Lupara”, created in an Excel database, the “Lupara district database”. sections.title: About the data

summary.text: Explains that institutional mortality data are often the only mortality source where civil registration is weak, while cautioning that they reflect the types of cases facilities receive. It stresses accurate cause-of-death recording using ICD coding.

sections.extract: Institutional mortality refers to deaths that occur while patients are admitted in hospitals and other inpatient facilities. In many countries, most deaths occur outside of health facilities, because of access challenges such as distance and lack of transport, as well as cultural, legal, security and financial issues. Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems are the official source of mortality

sections.title: Analysis

summary.text: Describes how to record causes of death and analyse institutional mortality by overall levels, leading causes and specific causes, using charts from the sample district. It discusses indicators such as stillbirths, neonatal and maternal deaths, case fatality rates and perioperative mortality. The section ends with factors affecting emergency unit mortality and the need to investigate unexpected rises.

sections.extract: step towards standardized cause of death reporting.2 The cause of death should be based on the final diagnosis, as this may be different from the admission diagnosis. Furthermore, the cause of death should be attributed to the underlying rather than the immediate cause. summary.text: Explains that facility morbidity data do not capture the full disease burden but can show patterns, and describes how diagnoses are coded and collected for outpatient and inpatient care.

sections.extract: Institutional morbidity refers to the diseases and health conditions for which people seek care at outpatient departments (OPD) or for which they are admitted to inpatient departments (IPD). Facility-based morbidity data have some similar limitations to mortality data. summary.text: Describes analysing leading causes of morbidity through ranked top-10 lists of outpatient and inpatient diagnoses, counting only new outpatient cases. It also covers tracking cases of selected diseases under surveillance to spot outbreaks. Charts from the fictitious district illustrate both analyses with interpretation questions.

sections.title: About the data

summary.text: Explains the concepts of health service utilization and access for a WHO guide on analysing routine health facility data, noting that utilization is often used as a rough proxy for access. It introduces three ways of analysing utilization and service availability data. Worked examples from the fictional Lupara district show outpatient visits by age and sex, with questions for the reader.

sections.extract: Service utilization1 refers to how often people use health services. Access refers to whether people are able to reach health services and use them. Access may be influenced by many factors such as availability and functionality of services, distances to facilities, cultural issues or financial barriers (e.g. out-of-pocket expenses for services and transport). Utilization is often used to provide a rough indication

sections.title: Core analysis

summary.text: Presents core analyses of service utilization, starting with outpatient visits per capita, for which no benchmark exists but trends should be monitored, illustrated with five years of Lupara district data. Further indicators include emergency unit use, inpatient utilization, surgical volume and service-specific availability. A map shows the hospitals providing caesarean sections, with dot size proportional to the number performed in 2019.

sections.title: About the data

summary.text: Defines service coverage and service outputs and explains that reported outputs can serve as proxies for coverage where reliable population denominators are lacking. It distinguishes coverage from quality indicators and explains why PMTCT testing is classed as a quality measure in this guidance.

sections.extract: This section discusses data on the coverage for essential health services or, where reliable denominators are not available, the outputs of these services. Coverage refers to the percentage of a target population that received a specific health intervention or service. sections.title: About the data

summary.text: Defines health service quality as delivery according to required standards and explains its importance for universal health coverage, noting that quality has many dimensions. It states that the section covers process and outcome indicators, with resource indicators left to the next chapter.

sections.extract: Health service quality refers to how well the service is delivered, i.e. whether it is provided according to required standards. Service quality is a critical component of UHC – without quality, coverage will not be effective and UHC cannot be achieved. Measuring quality is important both because the quality of a service or specific intervention determines its effectiveness and because community perceptions of

sections.title: Core analysis

summary.text: Works through core quality indicators, explaining what each reveals, such as early antenatal care, PMTCT testing and malaria preventive treatment in pregnancy. Others include caesarean section rates, immunization dropout and the HIV care cascade, plus inpatient and malaria case management measures. A Lupara district table of values ends with a question asking readers to spot suspicious findings, such as treatment percentages above 100%.

sections.title: About the data

summary.text: Explains that resources such as facilities, equipment, staff, medicines and finance are needed to deliver services and that resource data can shed light on performance. It notes that such data are often held outside routine information systems, for example in administrative and finance databases.

sections.extract: Resources (inputs or production factors) are necessary to provide health services. The main inputs for health service delivery include health facilities (infrastructure), equipment, staff, medicines and medical products, and financial resources. Financial resources are converted into the other resources or used in monetary form, for example, to cover operational costs. Information on the availability and use of

summary.text: Presents core analyses of health service resources, starting with facility density and distribution drawn from a master facility list, and hospital bed density. Further indicators assess efficiency through bed occupancy and length of stay, as well as health workforce availability and medicine stock-outs. The section ends with health finance, asking readers to interpret Lupara district's 2019 budget execution and plan spending for the last quarter.

sections.title: Annex 10: Answers to the questions in the guidance document

summary.text: Annex 10 gives model answers to the exercise questions throughout the routine health facility data guidance, based on the Lupara district dashboards. Early answers interpret patterns such as a December spike in institutional mortality and the age and sex distribution of outpatient visits. Later answers address coverage, quality and resource indicators, including data quality concerns. The last answer advises limiting fourth-quarter spending to essential activities given budget execution.
